excerpt: Paano magtanim ng lanzones? Here is how traditional Filipino farmers usually plant lansones (lanzones), step by step from getting the field ready to the harvest, with the day of each step and what to change for a higher yield.

heroImage.alt: Young fruit trees planted in straight rows on cleared red soil

blocks.title: This is the traditional way
blocks.text: This guide shows how traditional farmers usually plant lansones. Use it as a starting point. For a higher yield, update it: plant certified seed or clean planting material, test your soil, and follow the right spacing and fertilizer.

This guide shows how Filipino growers usually plant lanzones, today mostly grafted longkong or duku on native rootstock, under shade and care for it until the first fruits. It is for coconut farms, backyards and small orchards in places like Laguna, Camiguin and Mindanao.

Before you plant, get the field ready with our [land preparation guide for fruit and plantation trees](/land-preparation/fruit-tree-land-preparation). Then choose your seed or planting material with the [lansones varieties sold here](/crop-varieties/lanzones). If the leaves turn pale later on, the [lansones nutrient deficiency guide](/nutrient-deficiencies/lanzones-nutrient-deficiency) helps you find what is missing. For more on the crop, read [pagtatanim ng puno](/crops/pagtatanim-ng-puno).
When to plant lansones

Seedlings are planted as the rains begin, around May to July, under shade that is already growing. Lanzones needs a humid place with rain spread through most of the year and does poorly in long dry seasons. In Laguna the fruit is sold from about August to early December.
What you plant

Most growers now plant grafted longkong or duku joined to a hardy native Paete or Jolo seedling rootstock. Grafted plants are ready for the field about 6 to 12 months after grafting. Buy from a trusted nursery, since longkong leaves taste bland while Paete and Jolo leaves taste bitter when chewed. In the old way farmers planted Paete seedlings from seed, which can take 15 to 20 years to bear.
Paano magtanim ng lanzones, step by step
Well grown grafted longkong can bear at about 5 years. Many trees take longer, and Paete trees from seed take 15 to 20 years. The crop is ready about 5 years after planting.
Before planting (Bago magtanim)

items.title: 6 months before planting: Grow shade first
items.text: Lanzones needs shade when young, so plant banana, ipil ipil or kakawate in the field months before, or plant under coconut. The young trees should get filtered light, not full sun.

items.title: 14 days before planting: Mark and dig the holes
items.text: Mark the planting spots about 5 m apart each way. Dig holes about 25 cm wide and deep, or a little wider than the seedling bag.

blocks.text: Planting day (Pagtatanim)

items.title: Planting day: Plant the grafted seedling
items.text: Put about 50 to 100 g of complete fertilizer (14 14 14) or 16 20 0 in the hole and cover it with soil. Remove the bag, set the seedling at the depth it grew with the graft above the soil, firm the soil and water well.

blocks.text: Care while it grows (Pag aalaga)

items.title: Day 3: Keep the seedling shaded and moist
items.text: Make sure the young tree sits in light shade and mulch around it with dried leaves. Water in dry spells, since young lanzones dries out fast.

items.title: Day 30: Weed around the tree
items.text: Keep a clean circle around the young tree by hand. Keep grazing animals out so they do not pack the soil or eat the leaves.

items.title: Month 3: Feed the young tree
items.text: Feed the young tree lightly with complete fertilizer or manure every few months, more as it grows. Test the soil when you can and follow the result.

items.title: Month 4: Rub off rootstock shoots
items.text: Remove any shoot that grows below the graft, since it comes from the rootstock. Check every month in the first year.

items.title: Month 6: Check the bark for borers
items.text: Look at the trunk and branches for bark borer damage and loose, dead bark, and brush or scrape it off. Cut out dead twigs.

items.title: Month 12: Thin the shade and prune lightly
items.text: As the tree grows, cut back the temporary shade little by little so the tree gets more light. Remove water sprouts and dead or crowded inner twigs.

blocks.text: Harvest (Anihan)

items.title: Year 5: First fruits
items.text: Pick whole bunches when the fruits turn evenly yellow and taste sweet, cutting the stalk with a knife or shears. Handle the bunches gently and keep them in the shade.

blocks.text: Watering lansones, stage by stage

Lanzones here is rain fed in most farms, grown under coconut, banana or kakawate shade with a thick mulch of dried leaves. Young trees are watered in dry spells, and the few growers with water on hand irrigate bearing trees in the dry months for a better and earlier crop. A pail or hose into a mulched ring for young trees. Basin or sprinkler watering for bearing trees where a spring or pump is near. Water early in the morning.

blocks.title: Never let lansones go dry at these stages
blocks.text: The first two years, when young trees under stress grow slowly and recover poorly. Flowering and fruit set, when the flower clusters dry up in dry soil. Fruit growth, which needs even moisture for full, sweet bunches.

blocks.text:
**Without irrigation.** Plant at the start of the rains under shade that is already growing, and keep a thick mulch of dried leaves under the tree. Lanzones needs a humid place with rain spread through most of the year and does poorly where the dry season is long. On rain alone, the trees flower when the first heavy rains end the dry season, and the crop comes some months later.

**In the dry season.** Young trees about twice a week. Bearing trees about once a week from flowering to harvest, after the short dry spell that brings the flowers. Water when the leaves droop and fold by midday.

**In the rainy season.** Lanzones cannot stand flooding: plant on ground that drains, open drains from low spots, and keep water from standing around the trunk. Wet, shaded, crowded orchards get more bark disease and fruit rot, so thin the shade and prune water sprouts.

items: **Too little water:** Leaflets droop and fold by midday, older leaves yellow and fall, flower clusters dry up, and fruits stay small and sour.
**Too much water:** Yellow leaves and dying twigs on waterlogged ground, and more rotting bark and fruits in long rains.

blocks.text: To water better for a higher yield: Where you have water, let the soil dry at the start of the dry season and then water deeply: the trees flower and fruit weeks ahead of the rain fed crop, when prices are higher. Keep the shade, mulch and steady water through the first two years, the stage where most young lanzones are lost.
Spacing, water and fertilizer for lansones
Spacing
About 5 m by 5 m, one seedling a hole, or in the spaces between coconut trees. Holes about 25 cm wide and deep, or a little wider than the bag.
Water
Rain fed in most farms. Young trees are watered in dry spells and kept mulched and shaded. Growers with water on hand irrigate bearing trees in dry months for a better crop.
Fertilizer

About 50 to 100 g of complete fertilizer (14 14 14) or ammonium phosphate (16 20 0) in the hole at planting. Young trees get light feedings with complete fertilizer and manure, more each year. Some growers feed bearing trees with 17 0 17 and muriate of potash (0 0 60), giving the last dose about two months after the flowers come out. To read what a bag really gives, see our guide to [fertilizer for this crop](/blog/fertilizer-for-fruit-trees).
Care and harvest
Care while it grows

Planting under banana, kakawate, ipil ipil or coconut for shade, then thinning the shade as the tree grows. Weeding, mulching, keeping animals out, removing rootstock shoots, scraping loose bark and cutting borer damaged and dead twigs, and removing water sprouts.
When and how to harvest

Fruits are ready when the bunch has turned evenly yellow and the fruits taste sweet. Picking too early gives sour fruit. Whole bunches are cut with shears or a knife, packed loosely in baskets or crates and kept in the shade. In Laguna the season runs from about August to early December.
Common mistakes when planting lansones

items: Planting in full sun with no shade, so the young trees scorch and die.
Buying cheap seedlings that turn out to be ungrafted Paete instead of longkong.
Planting from seed and waiting 15 years or more for the first fruits.
Letting goats and cattle graze under the trees and pack the soil.
Ignoring loose bark and borers on the trunk.
Picking the bunches before they are fully yellow and sweet.

blocks.text: How to get a higher yield of lansones
The traditional way gets a crop, but small changes add up. These are the first things to change, one season at a time.

items: Plant grafted longkong or duku from an accredited nursery with known mother trees.
Test the soil and feed by the result, with potash for bearing trees.
Plan the shade: start with banana or kakawate and thin it as the trees grow.
Water during dry months so flowering and fruit set stay steady.
Scrape loose bark and scout for bark borers and scab every few months.
Prune water sprouts and crowded twigs after each harvest.

items.a: This guide shows how Filipino growers usually plant lanzones, today mostly grafted longkong or duku on native rootstock, under shade and care for it until the first fruits. Follow the steps above in order, from getting the field ready to the harvest, then change one thing at a time for a higher yield.

items.q: When do farmers plant lansones in the Philippines?
items.a: Seedlings are planted as the rains begin, around May to July, under shade that is already growing. Lanzones needs a humid place with rain spread through most of the year and does poorly in long dry seasons.

items.q: How far apart do you plant lansones?
items.a: About 5 m by 5 m, one seedling a hole, or in the spaces between coconut trees. Holes about 25 cm wide and deep, or a little wider than the bag.

items.q: How long before lansones can be harvested?
items.a: It is ready about 5 years after planting. Fruits are ready when the bunch has turned evenly yellow and the fruits taste sweet.

items.q: How often do you water lansones?
items.a: Planting to 3 months, planting day to month 3: Water well at planting, then every 2 to 3 days when no rain falls, in light shade. First and second year, month 3 to 24: About twice a week in the dry months, once a week on heavy soil. Years 3 to 5, before bearing, month 24 to 54: About once a week in the dry months where water is near. Young trees about twice a week.

items.q: What do you plant to grow lansones?
items.a: Most growers now plant grafted longkong or duku joined to a hardy native Paete or Jolo seedling rootstock. Grafted plants are ready for the field about 6 to 12 months after grafting.
